title: SIPF: Sampling Method for Inverse Protein Folding

problem.claim: Inverse protein folding generates a protein amino acid sequence from a 3D graph structure.

gap.claim: Existing inverse protein folding methods are mostly sequential generative models with limited uncertainty quantification and exploration ability across the protein space.

contributions.claim: SIPF formulates inverse protein folding as a sampling problem and uses two pretrained neural networks as an MCMC proposal distribution.
SIPF uses an adaptive sampling scheme to select sampling variables and an approximate target distribution as a surrogate for the unavailable target distribution.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Empirical studies report a 7.4% relative improvement in recovery rate over the best baseline.
Empirical studies report a 6.4% relative reduction in perplexity over the best baseline.

narrative_sequence.summary: Protein engineering has applications in drug discovery.
Inverse protein folding is a protein-design task that generates an amino acid sequence from a 3D graph structure.
Sequential generative approaches have limited uncertainty quantification and exploration across the protein space.
SIPF addresses the gap through sampling, neural-network MCMC proposals, adaptive variable selection, and an approximate target distribution.
The authors report improvements in recovery rate and perplexity over the best baseline.

source_observation.claim: The method formulates inverse protein folding as sampling and uses adaptive variable selection plus an approximate target distribution.

interpretation.claim: Sampling-based formulations can explicitly target exploration and address unavailable target distributions.

application.claim: For structured design problems with large spaces and unavailable targets, consider sampling proposals combined with adaptive selection and surrogate targets.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when the sampling strategy is preferable to sequential generative models beyond the reported study.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, baseline identities, or experimental settings.
The abstract does not provide details of the pretrained networks, sampling scheme, or approximate target distribution.
The abstract does not report uncertainty-quantification or exploration metrics.
